beliefs.title: AI is already in use.
beliefs.text: Staff already use AI tools, software vendors are adding AI to products organizations already pay for, and scammers already use AI against the people organizations serve. Not deciding is still a decision.
beliefs.quote: There is no neutral middle position. Inaction is a decision.

beliefs.title: AI reflects what it is given.
beliefs.text: AI produces its answers from what it was trained on and from what people give it. Good material and careful people get better results. Scattered material and careless use get worse ones. So the response to AI is mostly about people, not technology.
beliefs.quote: AI will mirror and amplify the humanity it finds sitting before it in any given interaction.

beliefs.title: Start with the mission and the people it serves.
beliefs.text: Decisions about AI should begin with what the organization exists to do and who it serves, not with what AI can do.
beliefs.quote: The answer is not primarily about AI. The answer is about whether organizations whose work depends on human covenant can carry that covenant into an age of machine fluency.

beliefs.title: Decisions need a clear process and clear authority.
beliefs.text: The people who contribute and the people who decide should be named in writing before any policy is drafted. The organization's governing body adopts the result.
beliefs.quote: A bad process can produce a good document and still fail, because the organization will not live by it.

beliefs.title: Learn before deciding.
beliefs.text: People cannot judge whether AI helps or harms their work without trying it on real tasks, with safeguards. This is true whether the organization ends up using AI a lot or not at all.
beliefs.quote: Technique without wisdom produces over-trust; wisdom without technique produces refusal.

beliefs.title: Protect people first.
beliefs.text: Protecting people from the risks of AI comes before looking for its benefits. Organizations owe this protection whatever they decide about their own use of AI.
beliefs.quote: The threats have to be prevented before the search for opportunities begins.

beliefs.title: Sort uses into prohibited, allowed with safeguards, and allowed.
beliefs.text: Some uses cause harm however carefully they are done. Most help only with safeguards. Some help clearly and harm no one. Movemental calls these red, yellow and green.
beliefs.quote: Take the AI out of the story. Look at what remains.

beliefs.title: Some work must be done by people.
beliefs.text: Care, judgments about people, and words published under a person's name must stay with people. AI may help prepare that work but may not replace the person.
beliefs.quote: The distinction between authorship and infrastructure matters, and we observe it carefully.

beliefs.title: An organization's information is its memory.
beliefs.text: Records, documents, teaching and know-how hold what an organization has learned about its people and its work. Most of it is scattered. Kept well, it is what makes AI useful. Handled carelessly, it puts people at risk.
beliefs.quote: Slop is not simply low quality. Slop is fragmentation, reflected and multiplied.

beliefs.title: People matter more than efficiency.
beliefs.text: Time saved by AI should go back to people, not simply into more work. Some work is slow because doing it forms people.
beliefs.quote: Formation and integrity matter more than efficiency.
beliefs.source: A Guide to AI and Credibility

beliefs.title: Work this out with others.
beliefs.text: No organization should decide this alone. Organizations learn faster and decide better with peers and with people who were wise before AI.
beliefs.quote: The antidote to any individual lack of wisdom about AI is doing the work alongside people whose wisdom predates AI.

beliefs.title: Organizations share responsibility for their communities.
beliefs.text: Government policy cannot reach every person, so each organization decides for itself how AI will affect the people it serves and its wider community.
beliefs.quote: The people who love their neighbors should help decide what AI becomes.

questions.title: What do I believe about AI?
questions.why: People who welcome AI and people who distrust it often see the same technology differently. Saying what you believe makes your other answers easier to understand.
questions.how: Tick every answer you agree with. Star the one closest to your view.

teach.heading: Why this question is about you
teach.text: Resolve starts with your own view. Your organization's decisions will be built from many people's views, and it helps to know your own first.

teach.heading: If you are not sure
teach.text: Choose the answers that match your experience so far. Most people choose more than one.

answers.text: I believe AI is a tool, like other software, that can be used well or badly.

ex: We should review AI features in our church management software the way we review any church software.
We should judge each AI tool by whether it serves our ministry, not by how new it is.
We should add AI tools to the same approval process we use for giving and attendance software.
We should evaluate AI tools on cost, security and fit, like any vendor.
We should review AI features in our donor database the way we review any software update.
We should add AI tools to our existing technology inventory and acceptable use policy.
We should review AI tools through the same IT approval process we use for our learning management system.
We should judge an AI tutor by what students actually learn, not by what the vendor promises.
We should add AI use to our existing academic integrity policy rather than writing a separate code.
We should review AI features in our membership database the way we review any other software.
We should put AI tools through the same procurement and security review as other office software.
We should advise member churches to judge AI features by the same standards as their church software.

answers.text: I believe AI repeats and magnifies what it is trained on and what we give it.

ex: We should check what AI tools say about our beliefs before we rely on them.
We should give AI only our own approved teaching when we ask it for study materials.
We should have a pastor review any AI summary of Scripture before it reaches a small group.
We should check what AI tools say about our mission and programs before relying on them.
We should test AI drafts of client letters for bias before using them.
We should keep our program information current so AI answers drawn from it are accurate.
We should give our AI research assistant only library sources our faculty have reviewed.
We should check AI study guides for bias before teachers hand them to students.
We should teach faculty that careless prompts and poor course materials produce poor AI answers.
We should test what AI tools say about our doctrine and polity before recommending them to member churches.
We should give any AI tool we offer our approved resources, not scattered drafts.
We should teach church planters that AI answers reflect their sources and the questions they are asked.

answers.text: I believe AI gives a few companies more control over work and information.

ex: We should ask who owns and profits from each AI tool our church adopts.
We should check what AI vendors do with our members' giving and prayer records.
We should keep our sermons and teaching in files we control, not only inside one vendor's platform.
We should ask who profits from each AI tool we adopt.
We should check what AI vendors do with the data of the people we serve.
We should avoid depending on one AI vendor for both case management and fundraising.
We should keep student records and course content on systems our school controls.
We should avoid building our curriculum around a single AI vendor we cannot easily leave.
We should ask faculty governance to review any AI contract that changes how teaching is done.
We should ask what each AI vendor does with the data of our member churches and missionaries.
We should avoid locking member churches into one AI vendor through our shared contracts.
We should keep ownership of our publications and archives when AI companies ask to license them.

answers.text: I believe AI puts important human things at risk if we do not protect them.

ex: We should name the parts of our ministry that AI may not touch.
We should protect hospital visits, prayer and discipleship from being replaced by automated messages.
We should keep our children's and youth ministry led by people, not AI tools.
We should name the parts of our work with clients that AI may not touch.
We should keep mentoring and camp counseling relationships between people, not apps.
We should protect face-to-face time between caseworkers and the families they serve.
We should keep faculty grading and commenting on student theses themselves.
We should protect spiritual formation groups and chapel from AI tools.
We should keep teachers, not AI tutors, at the center of our elementary classrooms.
We should name the parts of ordination, candidacy and member care that AI may not touch.
We should protect in-person visits between regional staff and member church pastors.
We should help member churches name the parts of their ministry they will keep free of AI.

answers.text: I believe AI can help people we could not otherwise reach.

ex: We should caption every service so members who are deaf or hard of hearing can follow.
We should use AI translation so families who speak other languages can follow announcements.
We should let a small church with no paid staff use AI to keep up with office work.
We should use AI to answer families in their own language.
We should offer AI audio and plain-language versions of our application forms.
We should use AI so our small relief team can respond faster after disasters.
We should offer AI-supported language study to distance students who cannot relocate to campus.
We should provide AI accessibility tools for students with documented learning disabilities.
We should use AI translation to help parents who do not speak English follow school news.
We should use AI translation so minority-language congregations receive our resources in their own language.
We should caption and transcribe our conference sessions for pastors who cannot attend.
We should offer approved AI tools to small member churches that have no paid staff.

take.head: AI repeats and magnifies what it is given. That is why each of the other answers can be true, depending on how it is used.

body.value: AI is trained on a very large amount of human writing, and it produces its answers from that training and from what a person or organization gives it. Careful use with good material can help a great deal. Careless use, poor material or bad intent produce worse results, faster.

So the other answers are not wrong. AI is a tool. It does give a small number of companies a great deal of control. It can wear away human care and judgment if no one protects them, and it can reach a family at two in the morning in their own language. Which of these happens in your organization depends mostly on the people using it.

We have noticed that how people react to AI often shows what they already believe about people. Those most worried are often worried about what humans have already produced. Those most hopeful are often hopeful about people for the same reason.
Why this matters for the rest of Resolve

If AI mostly reflects what it is given, the most important questions are about us: what we value, what we protect, how we keep our information and how we train our people. The questions that follow are in that order.

questions.title: What do I believe should guide our decisions about AI?
questions.why: Every AI policy rests on values. When values are not written down, hard cases turn into arguments with nothing to settle them.
questions.how: Tick every answer you agree with. Star the one you would point to first.

teach.heading: What we mean by values
teach.text: The convictions you would keep even if the technology changed completely. If a value would need rewriting every time a new AI model came out, it is a preference about tools, not a value.

teach.heading: If you are not sure
teach.text: Think of two good people in your organization who disagree about using AI. What would you point to in order to settle it?

answers.text: Scripture and our tradition.

ex: We should test every AI decision against our statement of faith.
We should study what Scripture says about wisdom, work and truth before setting our AI guidelines.
We should ask our denomination or tradition what it has taught about new technology.
We should check every AI use against our mission statement.
We should revisit our founding documents before writing our AI policy.
We should ask our board whether each AI use fits the faith commitments we were founded on.
We should have our theology faculty write the biblical basis for our AI policy.
We should test proposed AI uses in chapel and formation against our statement of faith.
We should draw on our tradition's teaching about vocation when deciding which faculty work AI may do.
We should test our AI guidance against our statement of faith and confessional standards.
We should ask our theological commission to review AI guidance before it goes to member churches.
We should ground our AI resources for member churches in our shared tradition, not vendor marketing.

answers.text: Love for our neighbors, including people outside our organization.

ex: We should ask how each AI use affects neighbors outside our congregation.
We should consider members and neighbors without smartphones or internet before any AI change.
We should make sure our AI choices do not put our neighbors' information at risk.
We should consider AI's effect on our neighborhood, not only our clients.
We should ask how our AI choices affect partner agencies and local volunteers.
We should weigh how our AI tools affect families who never enroll in our programs.
We should teach students to protect their families and churches from AI scams.
We should consider how our graduates' AI habits will affect the congregations they serve.
We should open our AI literacy evenings to parents and neighbors, not only enrolled families.
We should ask how our AI guidance affects the neighborhoods our member churches serve.
We should consider how our AI choices affect the communities where our missionaries live.
We should ask how our church planting tools affect people who are not yet part of any church.

answers.text: The good of the people we serve, before efficiency.

ex: We should drop any AI use that saves staff time but weakens pastoral care.
We should keep calling and visiting members in person even when an automated message would be faster.
We should judge AI in discipleship by its effect on people, not by hours saved.
We should drop any AI use that saves time but weakens care.
We should keep a person at intake even when AI could process applications faster.
We should judge AI in our youth programs by its effect on young people, not staff hours.
We should keep small writing seminars even if AI feedback would let us enlarge classes.
We should choose AI tools for what helps students learn, not for what saves the most staff time.
We should keep in-person advising even when an AI chatbot could answer most registration questions.
school.text: The good of our students, before efficiency.

ex: We should drop any AI use in member care that saves staff time but weakens care.
We should judge AI tools for member churches by their effect on congregations, not on our costs.
We should keep candidacy mentoring personal even if AI could process candidates faster.

answers.text: The trust people have placed in us.

ex: We should ask whether members would still trust us if they saw how we use AI.
We should protect prayer requests and confidences before any gain in efficiency.
We should never use AI in a way we would be unwilling to explain from the pulpit.
We should protect the trust of donors and clients before any gain.
We should ask whether families would still trust us if they saw how we use AI.
We should keep campers' and parents' information out of any tool we cannot vouch for.
We should honor the trust parents place in us by never sharing student data with AI vendors without consent.
We should keep our promises to donors about how their gifts fund teaching, not AI replacements.
We should protect the confidence students place in counselors and chaplains.
We should ask whether member churches would still trust us if they saw how we use AI.
We should protect the trust clergy place in us with their personnel files and pension records.
We should ask whether supporters would still trust our missionary updates if they knew how they were written.

answers.text: Evidence of what helps people and what harms them.

ex: We should check how an AI use is working after one season before expanding it.
We should ask other churches what actually happened when they used AI in ministry.
We should stop any AI use that we find is causing confusion or harm.
We should measure program results before and after any AI change.
We should track AI errors at intake and review them every month.
We should ask peer agencies for evidence before adopting an AI tool they recommend.
We should pilot AI tutoring in one course and measure learning before expanding it.
We should study how AI writing tools affect our students' reasoning before allowing them widely.
We should track whether AI-flagged early alerts actually help struggling students stay enrolled.
We should pilot AI tools with a few member churches and measure results before wider rollout.
We should collect evidence from regions using AI before writing guidance for every member church.
We should track whether AI translation actually helps partner churches understand our resources.

answers.text: The views of the people most affected by our decisions.

ex: We should include our teenagers in writing our AI rules.
We should ask older members how AI changes in communication would affect them.
We should ask members with disabilities which AI accessibility tools actually help them.
We should pay community members to advise our AI decisions.
We should include youth participants in writing the AI rules for our youth programs.
We should ask our client advisory council before any client-facing AI use.
We should put students on the committee that writes our AI policy.
We should ask parents what they want before introducing AI tools in our K-12 classrooms.
We should hear adjunct faculty before deciding how AI will change grading.
We should survey pastors and missionaries before issuing AI guidance.
We should include small and rural member churches on our AI guidance task force.
We should ask partner churches in other countries how our AI choices affect them.

take.head: Start with your mission and the people you serve, not with what AI can do. Write your values down before you write any rules.

body.value: Much AI guidance begins with what the technology can do and asks how to use it. We begin with what the organization exists for and who it serves: a congregation, a neighborhood, students, clients, families. The question is whether AI helps that work or gets in its way.

Our own starting point is love of neighbor. For a church, Scripture and tradition shape decisions about AI the way they shape every other decision. For a nonprofit, its mission does the same. For a school, it is what it hopes its students become.
Values that are not written down get replaced by the values built into the tools: speed, scale, engagement and cost. Those decide close cases unless something else is written first.
Evidence matters too
We would include evidence among your values, in support of them rather than in place of them. Evidence tells you what a tool does. Your values tell you whether you want it done.

questions.title: What should every organization do, even if it decides not to use AI?
questions.why: Some responsibilities apply whether an organization uses AI a lot, a little or not at all. This question names them before anyone discusses how much to use AI.
questions.how: Tick every answer you agree with. Star the one your organization should do first.

teach.heading: Can an organization avoid AI completely?
teach.text: It can decide not to use AI in its own work. It cannot avoid AI altogether. Most staff already use AI tools, usually without guidance. Vendors are adding AI to software organizations already use. Scammers already copy the voices of pastors and directors with AI to ask staff and members for money.

teach.heading: What this means for deciding not to use AI
teach.text: Deciding not to use AI can be the right decision. To make it responsibly, an organization still needs to know what is already happening, protect its people, and understand AI well enough to decide.

teach.heading: A question to ask about waiting
teach.text: Waiting can be wise. Our own writing asks whether a decision to wait is really a decision, or fear that has been put into words.

teach.heading: If you are not sure
teach.text: Ask which of these your organization could explain to a member, donor or parent if something went wrong next month.

answers.text: We should find out how AI is already being used in our organization, without blaming anyone.
answers.ask: Do we know how AI is already being used in our organization?

ex: We should ask every staff member and key volunteer which AI tools they use and for what.
We should list every AI feature already built into our church software.
We should ask our worship and communications teams to show how they already use AI, without blame.
We should ask every staff member which AI tools they use and for what.
We should list every AI feature already in our donor database and case management software.
We should ask volunteers and camp counselors which AI tools they use for our work.
We should survey faculty on how they already use AI in courses, with answers kept anonymous.
We should ask registrar, admissions and finance staff which AI tools they already use at work.
We should list the AI features already switched on in our learning platform and student systems.
We should ask every staff member in our national and regional offices which AI tools they use.
We should list the AI features already built into our membership, giving and credentialing software.
We should invite member churches to share how they already use AI, without judging their answers.

answers.text: We should protect our people from AI scams, cloned voices and fake images, and teach them to recognize these.
answers.ask: How are we protecting our people from AI scams, cloned voices and fake images?

ex: We should teach older members how to spot AI voice-cloning scam calls.
We should warn members that we will never ask for gift cards or money by text or email.
We should teach families to agree on a code word to check calls that sound like a relative.
We should warn clients about AI-driven benefit and immigration scams.
We should have staff confirm any urgent payment request from a leader by calling them back.
We should teach youth participants how to spot fake images and AI-made messages.
We should warn students and parents about cloned voice calls asking for tuition payments or money.
We should teach business office staff to confirm any payment request by calling a known number.
We should train teachers to recognize fake AI images of students and report them right away.
We should warn member churches about scams that use AI to impersonate our bishop or president.
We should require a callback to a known number before acting on any voice or video request for funds.
We should give member churches a short guide to protecting older members from AI voice scams.

answers.text: We should set rules for sensitive information right away.
answers.ask: What are our rules for sensitive information, and does everyone know them?

ex: We should keep pastoral notes and counseling records out of all AI tools.
We should never put prayer requests or children's names into free AI tools.
We should write a one-page rule on sensitive information for staff and volunteers this month.
We should allow client information only in our approved case management system for now.
We should keep survivors' and minors' information out of every AI tool until rules are set.
We should list the information staff may never paste into AI tools.
We should forbid putting student records, grades or counseling notes into unapproved AI tools.
We should tell faculty this week which student information may never enter a public chatbot.
We should keep admissions files and financial aid documents out of AI tools until we approve one.
We should forbid entering missionaries' names or locations into public AI tools.
We should keep clergy personnel, misconduct and pension records out of all AI tools.
We should give member churches a model rule for keeping pastoral notes out of AI tools.

answers.text: We should learn enough to decide well, by trying AI on low-risk work.
answers.ask: Who among us will try AI on low-risk work, so we can decide well?

ex: We should let staff try AI on office tasks before deciding anything about ministry.
We should have our administrator try AI on the bulletin layout for one season.
We should let a few volunteers test AI on room scheduling before anyone else uses it.
We should give a small team a few months to try AI on internal work.
We should try AI on grant research and meeting notes before any client-facing use.
We should let our development team test AI on newsletter formatting first.
We should let a few staff try AI on event schedules and room bookings this term.
We should have faculty test AI on drafting a sample syllabus before deciding classroom rules.
We should try AI summaries of public committee minutes before using it with any student work.
We should let a small team in our national office try AI on internal work for three months.
We should test AI on conference logistics before considering it for anything involving people.
We should pilot AI tools with a few willing member churches before offering them more widely.

answers.text: We should tell our people where we stand on AI, even if we have not decided yet.
answers.ask: When will we tell our people where we stand on AI?

ex: We should explain our current AI position to the congregation this year.
We should tell volunteers in writing which AI uses are allowed while we decide the rest.
We should have our pastor say plainly from the pulpit where we stand on AI so far.
We should publish a short AI statement for donors and clients.
We should explain our current AI rules at the next all-staff and volunteer meeting.
We should tell parents how our youth programs and camps use AI this season.
We should tell students at orientation where the school currently stands on AI in coursework.
We should send parents a short note on our current AI rules while the full policy is drafted.
We should ask every instructor to state in the syllabus what AI use is allowed this term.
We should send member churches a short statement of where we stand on AI this year.
We should tell our missionaries and field staff our current AI position, even before final guidance.
We should explain our AI position from the platform at our next annual gathering.

answers.text: We should set a date to decide, and a date to review our decisions.
answers.ask: When will we decide, and when will we review what we decide?

ex: We should put AI guidelines on the elders' agenda for a decision by a set date.
We should review our AI decisions at every annual congregational meeting.
We should set a date for our church plant's leadership team to decide on AI.
We should put AI on the board agenda for a recorded vote.
We should set a date this fiscal year to adopt an AI policy.
We should review our AI decisions each year when we prepare our annual report.
We should set a date for the trustees to adopt our AI policy this academic year.
We should review our AI rules at the end of every semester.
We should put an annual AI policy review on the faculty senate calendar.
We should put AI guidance on the agenda of our next assembly or synod for a vote.
We should review our AI decisions at every annual meeting.
We should set a date by which our national office will adopt its own AI policy.

take.head: All six. These are the basic responsibilities. Every responsible approach to AI, including deciding not to use it, depends on them.

body.value: We do not think every approach to AI is equally sound at the start. One approach is clearly unsound: making no decision. It is also the most common. In the research we rely on, about nine in ten churches and nearly half of nonprofits have no AI policy, while most of their staff already use AI.

So before any organization decides how much to use AI, we would ask it to do six things. Find out what is already happening. Protect people from AI scams, which reach your members whether or not you use AI yourself. Set rules for sensitive information. Learn enough by trying AI to make a real decision. Tell your people where you stand. Set a date to decide and a date to review.
Deciding not to use AI

We respect organizations that decide not to use AI for reasons of conscience. We also want to be honest with them. Your staff use AI, your vendors include it, and it is used on the people you serve. Deciding not to use AI is a real decision about your own work. It does not remove these six responsibilities.

A decision not to use AI is also more trustworthy when it is informed. Our guides say to experiment before you adopt or refuse. That does not mean everyone must use AI. A person who objects on conscience can take full part in these six steps, for example by helping protect people and set rules, while others in the organization do the testing. Either way, the organization is making decisions about AI. The only question is whether it makes them on purpose.

questions.title: Who should make decisions about AI, and who is accountable?
questions.why: People can agree on what should happen and still disagree about who should decide. Settling this first makes later decisions legitimate.
questions.how: Tick every answer your organization should hold. Star the one that matters most. Wording changes for each kind of organization.

teach.heading: Three roles
teach.text: Who decides: the person or body with authority to approve AI policy. Who is consulted: the people whose work and lives are affected. Who is accountable: one named person who makes sure decisions are carried out, reviewed, and corrected when something goes wrong.

teach.heading: If you are not sure
teach.text: Think of how your organization made its last major decision, such as a building project or a change in programs. AI decisions probably belong with the same people.

answers.text: Our governing body should make the final decision, after hearing from our people. (Board, elders or trustees.)

ex: We should bring our AI guidelines to the elders for a recorded vote.
We should have our church council hear from staff and members before adopting an AI policy.
We should have one AI policy approved by our elders for every campus.
church.text: Our governing body should make the final decision, after hearing from our people. (Elders, session, vestry or church council.)

ex: We should have the board approve our AI policy.
We should gather comments from staff and our client advisory council before the board votes.
We should report our AI use to the board every quarter.
nonprofit.text: Our board should make the final decision, after hearing from our people.

ex: We should have the trustees adopt our AI policy after the faculty senate and student government comment.
We should bring any AI use in admissions or student records to the board for approval.
We should have the board's academic affairs committee review AI policy each year.
school.text: Our board of trustees should make the final decision, after hearing from faculty, staff and students.

ex: We should bring our AI standards to the assembly for a recorded vote.
We should have our board approve the AI policy for our national and regional offices.
We should have our council adopt AI guidance only after hearing from member churches.
network.text: Our governing body should make the final decision, after hearing from our people. (Board, assembly, synod or council.)

answers.text: We should decide together as a whole community, not leaders alone.

ex: We should hold listening sessions with members before setting AI guidelines.
We should discuss AI questions in small groups before the church decides.
We should decide our AI policy at a congregational meeting, not by leaders alone.
We should include staff, volunteers and clients in shaping our AI policy.
We should share our draft AI policy with all staff for comment before adoption.
We should hold open sessions for volunteers and families before setting AI rules.
We should write our AI policy through faculty, staff and students meeting together.
We should hold open campus forums before adopting AI rules for coursework.
We should invite parents, teachers and staff to shape our school's AI policy together.
We should ask member churches to discern AI together before we issue guidance.
We should hold regional listening sessions with pastors and lay leaders before drafting AI guidance.
We should bring draft AI guidance to the full assembly for discussion, not only to staff.

answers.text: We should follow our denomination's or network's guidance, and adapt it to our setting.

ex: We should adopt our denomination's AI guidance and add our own rules for pastoral care.
We should ask our network what AI guidance it gives church plants before writing our own.
We should follow our denomination's data rules for any AI that touches member records.
We should adopt our national affiliate's model AI policy and adapt it to our programs.
We should meet our accreditor's AI requirements before any client-facing use.
We should follow our denomination's AI guidance for our chaplaincy and spiritual care.
nonprofit.text: We should follow our national affiliate's, network's or denomination's guidance, and adapt it to our setting.

ex: We should adopt our sponsoring denomination's AI guidance and add rules for our classrooms.
We should start from our accrediting association's AI standards and fit them to our degree programs.
We should use our Christian school association's model AI policy and adjust it for our grade levels.
school.text: We should follow guidance from our sponsoring denomination, network or school association, and adapt it to our setting.

ex: We should follow our communion's guidance on AI and adapt it for our member churches.
We should adopt our mission alliance's AI standards and add rules for our field teams.
We should adapt the shared AI guidance of our ecumenical partners rather than write ours alone.
network.text: We should follow the guidance of the wider body we belong to, such as a communion or alliance, and adapt it to our setting.

answers.text: We should consult the people most affected before we decide.

ex: We should ask parents before AI is used in anything involving children.
We should hear from care ministry volunteers before AI is used in follow-up with members.
We should include Spanish-speaking members in decisions about AI translation.
We should hold a forum for program participants before any AI decision.
We should ask parents before AI is used in anything involving their children.
We should ask frontline caseworkers before AI changes how intake works.
We should ask students how proposed AI rules would affect their coursework before we decide.
We should consult counselors and chaplains before any AI tool touches student care.
We should hear from teachers before choosing AI tools for their classrooms.

answers.text: We should make one named person accountable for our AI decisions.

ex: We should name one elder accountable for our AI decisions.
We should list one staff contact for AI questions in our member handbook.
We should have a pastor, not only a technology volunteer, answer for our AI use.
We should name one board member responsible for AI oversight.
We should name one staff member responsible for every AI tool we use.
We should make our executive director accountable to the board for AI decisions.
We should name the academic dean accountable for AI use in teaching and grading.
We should make our head of school responsible for AI policy across all grade levels.
We should name one person accountable for AI tools used with student records.
We should name one senior officer accountable for all our AI decisions.
We should appoint one staff officer to coordinate AI across our agencies.
We should tell member churches which named officer is accountable for the AI tools we provide.

answers.text: When AI causes harm, we should tell the people affected and put it right before anything else.

ex: We should tell the congregation if AI mishandled member information.
We should contact a family directly if an AI error affected their child's information.
We should correct and apologize publicly for any AI error in a sermon or announcement.
We should tell clients when an AI error affected their case.
We should correct any AI error in a client's file before any other work.
We should tell donors directly if an AI tool exposed their information.
We should tell students right away when an AI grading error changed their marks, and correct them.
We should notify affected families first if student data is exposed through an AI tool.
We should withdraw any AI admissions screening that treated applicants unfairly and review those decisions.
We should tell member churches promptly if AI mishandled their data in our systems.
We should tell a candidate directly if an AI error affected their credentialing file, and correct it.

take.head: Decide who decides before you decide anything else. Make AI decisions the way you already make decisions of similar importance, and never leave accountability to a vendor.

body.value: The most common problem we see is not a bad decision about AI. It is AI decisions made by whoever knows the most about technology, or by no one. Every organization already has a way to make important decisions: a board, elders, a council, a congregation, faculty governance. AI decisions belong there.

Name the contributors and the decision makers in writing before anything is drafted. Contributors are the four to seven people whose work and views should shape the policy. Decision makers are the people with authority to approve it. When these roles are unclear, disagreements about who has authority tend to surface halfway through and stall the work.

The leader of the organization should not write the policy alone. The leader is responsible for making sure the process is fair and keeps moving. When the governing body approves the policy, the organization has committed to it together.
Accountability

Something will go wrong. When it does, the organization is responsible, not the vendor. Name one person who makes sure someone is always responsible, and decide now that the person harmed comes first: tell them the truth, put it right, then fix the cause.
Movemental does not decide for you

We can help an organization see what its people believe and lay out its options. We will not make the decision, and no count of Resolutions makes it either. Nothing is adopted until the people with authority adopt it.

answers.text: We should approve each use of AI separately, start small, and review it regularly.

ex: We should try each AI use for one season, then review it with the elders.
We should require a short written request before any ministry adopts an AI tool.
We should start with captions on Sunday and decide later about any other AI use.
We should require a short written proposal before adopting any AI tool.
We should pilot each approved AI use in one program for three months, then review it.
We should end each approved AI use unless the board renews it after review.

We should have our AI task force approve each new use and report to the assembly yearly.

answers.text: We should treat AI like other software, under the policies we already have.

ex: We should add AI to our existing technology, privacy and child safety policies.
We should review AI tools the way we review any church software.
We should have staff request AI tools through our usual budget process.
We should add AI to our existing technology and privacy policies.
We should send AI tools through our normal vendor review.
We should cover AI tools in new staff orientation like any other software.
We should let campus IT approve AI tools through normal software procurement.
We should apply our existing data privacy and academic integrity policies to AI.
We should treat AI features in our student information system like any other software update.
We should handle AI tools through our standard procurement and IT security review.
We should add AI to our existing technology, privacy and safeguarding policies.
We should include AI in the technology guidance we already give member churches.

answers.text: We should adopt AI quickly wherever it helps the people we serve.

ex: We should caption services live with AI and correct errors afterward.
We should start using AI translation for newcomers now rather than wait.
We should use AI so our volunteer-run office can respond to visitors within a day.
We should start using AI translation for clients now rather than wait.
We should use AI routing now so relief supplies reach more families.
We should use AI to shorten application wait times this year and review errors weekly.
We should give every student AI tools for language study this year.
We should offer AI-supported courses to students who cannot move to campus.
We should provide AI tutoring for students who cannot afford private tutors.
We should provide AI translation to partner churches with no staff now rather than wait.
We should release AI guidance for member churches now and update it every year.
We should give every missionary approved AI tools this year and adjust as we learn.

take.head: We believe the third answer is right for most organizations: approve each use separately, start small, and review it regularly. We take the other answers seriously.

body.value: AI is not one thing. A church can rightly refuse AI in preaching and use it for translation. A nonprofit can keep it out of every conversation with a client and use it to prepare grant reports. That is not inconsistent. It is judgment applied to each use, which suits a technology that changes every few months. Most uses help only with safeguards, and those safeguards can only be set one use at a time.

Faithfulness does not require using AI. It requires deciding about it. An organization that thinks it through carefully and decides to use very little AI has done what we are asking. What we oppose is drifting into a position: adopting AI that no one decided to adopt, or refusing it without ever examining the question.
Each of the other answers can be sound under one condition:

value: Not using AI is sound when it comes from real consideration and the basic responsibilities are met. It is not sound when it is a way of avoiding the question.
Administrative use only works when the organization writes down exactly which work counts as core mission work, so staff can tell where the line is.
Treating AI like other software works only if existing policies cover tools that write, speak and make recommendations. Most were written before these tools existed, so check them first.
Adopting quickly works when the people who would bear the risk have a say, a person is always reachable, and mistakes can be undone.

body.value: Speed

We would protect people quickly and adopt tools slowly. Protection cannot wait. Adoption should go one task at a time, with a set trial period and a decision at the end to keep, change or stop. Waiting is not automatically safe either: a family who needed translation went without it, and a staff member burned out on work a tool could have handled. Count those costs too.

questions.title: What work should always be done by people?
questions.why: Before deciding what AI may do, decide what it must not replace. This is the work that should stay with people even when AI could do it faster.

teach.heading: Helping is not replacing
teach.text: This does not mean AI can never help. AI might help a pastor research a passage or a caseworker find a form. What stays with people is the care, the judgment and the responsibility.

teach.heading: If you are not sure
teach.text: Think of the part of your organization's work you would least want someone to discover was done by AI. Start there.

answers.text: Any work with children, or care that depends on a personal relationship.

ex: We should have only people, never AI, teach and care for our children and youth.
We should keep hospital and homebound visits personal, with no AI substitute.
We should have a person, not a chatbot, follow up with first-time guests.
We should keep AI note-takers out of counseling and support groups.
We should have only people, never AI, mentor and supervise young people in our programs.
We should keep camp counselors, not AI apps, as the people campers turn to for help.

We should keep field education supervision a relationship between a supervisor and a student.
We should keep mentoring and advising conversations between faculty and their advisees.
We should have only people, never AI, lead our youth camps and children's events.
We should keep AI out of member care for our missionaries and clergy families.
We should recommend that member churches keep AI out of children's ministry and youth mentoring.

answers.text: Every decision about a person, including who receives help, membership, admission or employment.

ex: We should have elders, not AI, decide on membership and church discipline.
We should have the benevolence team, not AI, decide who receives financial help.
We should have people, not AI, screen and choose staff and volunteer leaders.
church.text: Every decision about a person, including who receives help, membership, leadership roles or employment.

ex: We should never let AI decide who receives emergency assistance.
We should keep AI out of hiring and volunteer screening decisions.
We should have a person review every application before anyone is denied services.
nonprofit.text: Every decision about a person, including who receives help, who joins our programs, or employment.

ex: We should never let AI rank or reject applicants for admission.
We should have a dean, not AI, decide and communicate academic dismissal.
We should keep AI out of tenure, promotion and faculty hiring decisions.

We should never use AI to screen job applicants for our national or regional offices.
We should have people, not AI, decide which church planters and member churches receive grants.

answers.text: Pastoral care, counseling and spiritual direction.

ex: We should never use AI chatbots to give pastoral counsel or spiritual direction.
We should keep AI note-takers out of counseling sessions and prayer meetings.
We should have a pastor or trained member respond to every request for care.
We should have only trained staff provide counseling, never an AI chatbot.
We should keep AI out of chaplaincy visits and prayer with clients.
We should have a person answer every crisis call, even with long waits.
We should keep AI out of student counseling and chaplaincy sessions.
We should keep spiritual direction for seminarians face to face with a trained director.
We should have a person, not a chatbot, answer students who reach out in crisis.
We should have a person, not AI, answer our clergy care line.
We should never route missionaries' care requests through AI first.
We should keep AI out of the counseling and coaching we offer pastors in crisis.
network.text: Pastoral care, member care, counseling and spiritual direction.

answers.text: Preaching and teaching, and anything published under a person's name.

ex: We should have our pastors write their own sermons.
We should never publish an article or devotional under a pastor's name that AI wrote.
We should have small group leaders prepare their own teaching rather than read AI scripts.
We should have staff write their own trainings and talks for youth and volunteers.
We should never publish AI-written pieces under our executive director's name.
We should write our testimony to lawmakers ourselves.
nonprofit.text: Teaching and public speaking on our behalf, and anything published under a person's name.

ex: We should have chapel speakers prepare their own sermons.
We should have faculty write and deliver their own lectures.
We should require students to write their own sermons and exegesis papers.
We should never send AI-written letters in our bishop's or president's name.
We should have people write the sermons and addresses given at our assemblies.
We should require named authors to write the curriculum we publish for member churches.

answers.text: Work that helps people learn and grow, even when AI would be faster.

ex: We should keep members reading Scripture themselves rather than relying on AI summaries.
We should have new believers work through discipleship lessons with a person, not an AI tutor.
We should have students in confirmation class write their own answers without AI.
We should have new caseworkers learn intake interviews without AI assistance.
We should keep AI out of reflective supervision and staff mentoring.
We should have youth in job programs write their own applications with a mentor's help.
We should teach Greek and Hebrew without AI translation tools.
We should have students write first drafts themselves in writing courses.
We should keep elementary math practice on paper with teacher feedback.
We should keep AI out of candidates' ordination papers and theological reflection.
We should keep church planter assessment and training in person, even when AI would be faster.
We should have ordination candidates write their exams in the room.

take.head: Keep decisions about people and personal care with people. AI may help prepare that work. It may not replace the person doing it.

body.value: AI can gather information, prepare options and point out what needs attention. But when a decision is about a person, such as whether to help them, admit them, discipline them or hire them, that person deserves someone who can explain the decision, can be persuaded, and is responsible for the result.

Personal care is the second line. A hospital visit, a hard conversation, a prayer or a welcome matters because a person does it. Where children are involved, or care depends on trust, a person must be there. A quick answer at two in the morning can still be care when no person is available, as long as no one is misled about who answered and a person can always be reached.
The third line is authorship. AI can help draft. A named person must read, approve and be responsible for anything sent in the organization's name.
Write it down

Our field guide recommends a written list of care boundaries: the specific kinds of work that must be done by a person, the kinds where AI may help a person but not replace them, and the reason for each. Without a written list, these boundaries tend to wear away one exception at a time.

questions.title: What uses of AI should we prohibit?

answers.text: Letting people think they are dealing with a person when it is AI.

answers.text: Putting sensitive information into AI tools that do not protect it.

We should never use AI risk scores to decide which families get services first.
We should not use AI proctoring that watches students through their webcams.

answers.text: Copying a real person's voice or image with AI, or publishing AI writing as a person's own.

ex: We should never create an AI version of our pastor's voice or face.
We should never publish AI-written prayers or articles under a member's name.
We should never make AI images of real members without their knowledge and consent.
We should never clone a real person's voice for our appeals.
We should never use AI-generated images of the people we serve in fundraising.
We should never send AI-written letters to officials under supporters' names.
We should never create AI voice or video copies of faculty, even for online courses.
We should not publish AI-written articles under our president's or faculty's names.

answers.text: Using AI in ways that treat people unfairly because of race, age, disability, language or income.

ex: We should check that AI translation serves every language group in our church equally.
We should never use AI tools that sort applicants for church jobs by age or background.
We should keep a non-digital way to give, register and get help for members without internet.
We should test any AI eligibility tool for bias before using it with clients.
We should refuse AI tools that work poorly for clients with limited English.
We should check that our AI chatbot works for clients who use screen readers.
We should not use AI admissions tools that disadvantage applicants by race, disability or income.

take.head: Keep this list short and absolute. Then set up your tools so these uses are not possible, rather than relying on people to remember the rules.

body.value: We hold all six. Movemental's own public commitments include several of them: we do not imitate people with AI, we do not use AI in place of human care, and we do not use AI to decide who has access to what we offer. Each of these damages trust in a way that is very hard to repair, and no amount of convenience outweighs that.
Unfair treatment

AI learns from records that already contain unfairness. A tool that sorts applications, translates or flags people as risks can treat them differently by race, age, disability, language or income without anyone intending it. Wherever AI touches information about people, check its results for this before relying on them.
Make it impossible, not just forbidden

A rule against pasting counseling notes into a chatbot depends on every person remembering it on every busy day. Setting up your systems so those notes cannot reach the chatbot does not. We prefer the second whenever possible: control what each tool can see, what it can send and what it is connected to.
Each prohibited use also needs a plain statement, a reason people understand, a person responsible for it, and a known consequence when it is broken.
Keep the list short
If everything is prohibited, people start working around the policy. Most uses of AI need judgment rather than a ban. They belong in the next question.

take.head: Most AI decisions happen here. For each use, name the safeguard and the person who checks it, and try it on a small scale before expanding it.

body.value: Movemental sorts AI uses into three groups, and most uses fall into this middle group: real benefit, but only with enough safeguards. Drafts a person reviews before sending. Research that is checked against sources. Help that never takes the place of the people involved.
A few safeguards cover most cases:

value: A named person approves it. Someone reviews the result, edits it and is responsible for it.
A person can be reached. No one's only contact with your organization is AI.
Facts are checked. Claims, numbers and quotations are verified before anyone relies on them.
Knowledge and consent. The people we serve know when AI is part of their care and can say no.
Trial and review. A use is tried for a set period and then kept, changed or stopped.
Review before adoption. A new tool is checked against your policy, including what it does with your information, before anyone uses it.

body.value: When unsure, slow down

The same tool can carry different risks. An internal summary is not a public statement, and a draft you will rewrite is not a post you will publish almost unchanged. When the result will shape people or represent you publicly, review it yourself. When it is internal and low-risk, less review is needed. teach.text: Imagine the same work without AI. If what remains is people doing valuable work that AI helped them do faster or for more people, the use is good.

body.value: Making documents searchable, captioning and translating for access, and finding patterns that would take weeks by hand are clear benefits with no real harm. We use AI for work like this ourselves and encourage organizations to do the same.

Generic AI gives generic results. A chatbot that knows nothing about your organization writes what any organization might say. questions.title: How should we protect and use our organization's information?
questions.why: Organizations hold years of information about their people and their work. How that information is kept decides both what is at risk and how useful AI can be.

teach.heading: What we mean by information
teach.text: Not only data in the narrow sense. Records, documents, sermons and teaching, reports, decisions, relationships and know-how: what an organization has learned about its people and its work over the years. Much of it is scattered across files, inboxes and people's memories.

teach.heading: Why AI makes this urgent
teach.text: AI produces answers from what it is given. Given scattered, incomplete information about your organization, it fills the gaps with confident guesses. Given your own information, gathered and organized, it can give useful answers no generic tool can. The same information that needs protecting is what makes AI useful.

take.head: Your information is your organization's memory: what it has learned about its people and its work over many years. Protect it because it is about people. Organize it because it is what makes AI accurate about you.

body.value: Most discussion of data and AI is about risk, and the risk is real. Donor records, pastoral notes, information about children, immigration status and health details need the most care. Start by knowing what you hold and sorting it by sensitivity, so the most sensitive information never reaches an outside AI tool and everything else goes only to tools whose terms protect it.

That is only half of it. An organization's records, teaching, history and know-how are what it has learned over the years. In most organizations they are scattered: sermons no one can search, grant reports filed by year, important know-how in one person's head. We have told churches plainly that the real value here is memory, not efficiency. An organization committed to continuity can still forget most of what it knows.
AI repeats what it is given

Ask AI about an organization whose information is scattered, and it builds an answer from whatever pieces it can find. The result sounds right but is not accurate. People call this AI slop, and it comes from scattered information. Give the same tool the organization's own information, organized and complete, and it can answer from what the organization actually knows, with sources.
This is why we say gathering and organizing information is not just preparation. It is the main work. Real value comes where an organization's actual work meets its own organized information.
A caution

Organizing information can also be used to build an organization's own name and reach. In the story of Babel, people built something unified for their own sake. At Pentecost, people were understood in their own languages. Organize your information to serve your people and your neighbors, not to replace your people with it.

Any of these may sometimes be right, but none should happen by default. We would not cut jobs based on projected savings. We would tell people early if their roles may change, and let them help decide how. For small organizations it is different: AI may make possible work they could never hire for, and that should be said openly.
People who object on conscience

A person who declines AI from sincere conviction should be respected, not just tolerated. They should have another way to do their work, and their choice should never count against them. Organizations need these people because they notice what is being lost.

Avoidance is different. Some people avoid a workflow the organization has agreed on because they are overwhelmed, worried about looking unskilled, or unsure what is allowed. take.head: Teach people to check AI and use judgment first, then skills. Learn together, and keep some work free of AI so people stay able to think for themselves.

body.value: Checking first. AI gives wrong answers as confidently as right ones. Teaching people to check what AI tells them against sources and people they trust protects them and the people they serve. (Teaching people to recognize AI scams is covered in question 03, because every organization owes it whatever it decides.)
Judgment second. When should I use AI, and when should I not? What should I never give it? How do I check its answers? These questions apply to every tool.

Skills third. Training everyone, not only the most interested, keeps an organization from splitting into people who can use AI and people who cannot. Most of the skill is clear communication: saying what you want, giving enough background, knowing what a finished result looks like, and revising.
Avoiding dependence

Our training guide names three things to watch for in people who use AI a lot: tiredness of a different kind, a growing sense of working with someone rather than something, and a slow change in what seems like good writing or sound reasoning. None of these is a reason not to use AI. All are reasons to use it with care. Think first, keep some work free of AI, and talk together about how the tools are affecting your people.

Finally, everyone is new to this. AI tools as most people use them are only a few years old. Organizations that learn together and share what worked and what failed learn faster and more wisely than people learning alone.

take.head: Churches, nonprofits and schools should help decide how AI affects their communities. Protect your neighbors, work with others, and share what you learn.

body.value: Government policy cannot reach every person, and technology companies are not designed to. The decisions that most affect how AI touches ordinary lives are being made in congregations, agencies and classrooms. If churches, nonprofits and schools do not help lead, the people they serve will be left out of those decisions.

At a minimum, every organization owes its community protection. Teaching people to recognize scams, fake images and manipulation costs little and protects many, especially older people, isolated people and people new to a language or country.

Responsibility also includes cost to creation. Training and running AI uses large amounts of electricity and water. That is not a reason to refuse all AI, but it is a reason to use it where it matters and not by habit.
Work with others

Movemental exists partly to make this possible: a network of trusted leaders and organizations working through the same questions together, sharing what worked and what failed, while staying rooted in their own places. One organization's tested decision can save many others from guessing. We would ask every organization to share what it learns and to learn from people whose wisdom came before AI.
Different ways to respond

For some organizations, the best example will be a careful, humane way of using AI that others can see. For others, it will be public advocacy for people harmed by AI. Both are good responses. What we hope no organization does is assume this responsibility belongs to someone else.
